children: India is a market with a lot of promise, with the current focus being on building sales capabilities - CEO Sansbury

Cloudera's top leadership used Evolve26 Singapore to unpack the thinking behind Anywhere Cloud, the platform the company is positioning as its answer to the swing back towards hybrid infrastructure. Across three separate conversations with CTO Sergio Gago and CPO Leo Brunnick, CRO Brian Rosso and APJ SVP Remus Lim, and finally CEO Charles Sansbury and CBO Abhas Ricky, a consistent story emerged: A Chief Executive who is aware of what needs to be done, three acquisitions in just over a year, a customer base pulling back from all-in cloud bets, sharper scrutiny of AI spend, and a bet that owning 30 exabytes of critical enterprise data is a bigger moat than any single product.
The Making Of Anywhere Cloud

Cloudera's newly launched Anywhere Cloud platform, unveiled at its annual global summit, EVOLVE26, did not begin life as a single grand plan. According to Sansbury, it was the product of three separate acquisitions made in roughly 14 months, each one solving an immediate problem before the pieces came together into what the company now calls its core differentiator.

The first was Verta, brought in around two years ago for its inferencing and applied AI expertise. The second was Octopai, a data lineage and metadata management company, now rebranded internally as Cloudera Data Lineage, addressing what Sansbury described as a governance gap customers kept raising: they needed lineage, metadata and data quality handled natively rather than bolted on.

The third, and by his own account the most consequential, was Taikun, a Prague-based Kubernetes and cloud-orchestration company Cloudera acquired to containerise its own platform rather than build on top of a dominant third-party containerisation vendor. Brunnick, CPO, in the first roundtable, said Cloudera looked at roughly four candidate companies globally before settling on Taikun, the foundation of Anywhere Cloud’s data lineage solution.

What began as a tactical fix turned out to include a Kubernetes-based orchestration layer that could serve as a single, unified control plane across public cloud, private data centres, sovereign clouds and air-gapped environments. This ‘control plane’ became Anywhere Cloud. “The technology we acquired from Taikun was so powerful and extendable, and it met an emerging market need”, added Sansbury. He called it "effectively another branch" of the product roadmap, in his words, arguably the most important of the three deals.

He was explicit that none of the three acquisitions was done for revenue. "We weren't buying standalone businesses," was the substance of his framing, twice repeated in different phrasing across the roundtable - ‘the intent was to accelerate research and development that would otherwise have taken years to build organically, essentially treating M&A as a tool to accelerate R&D'.

Asked whether more acquisitions were coming, Sansbury said Cloudera has what it needs to execute its current roadmap over the next 12 months, but remains open to small, tactical ‘tuck-in’ deals, i.e., companies with proven technology and product-market fit that haven't yet reached commercial scale. “Nothing currently under consideration”, Sansbury added.
Charles Sansbury, CEO, Cloudera
The Pendulum Is Swinging Back To Hybrid: Here Is Why

The clearest, most repeated theme across all three sessions was that the "move everything to the cloud" consensus of five to six years ago has broken. CTO Sergio Gago cited an internal survey of roughly 1,500 data leaders, CDOs and CIOs globally, in which around 66 per cent said they are moving at least part of their AI and data workloads back toward on-premises infrastructure, a trend he said was especially pronounced in Europe and parts of South America.

Gago pointed to two forces driving this. First, the economics of inference. Token and GPU costs at scale are pushing enterprises to want their own GPU capacity rather than remain fully dependent on hyperscaler pricing.
Second, sovereignty. Enterprises and regulators are increasingly uncomfortable depending on a single cloud provider domiciled in a single country.

Anywhere Cloud's pitch is full optionality, i.e., the ability to move workloads between public clouds, private data centres and air-gapped environments through a single control plane, without a rip-and-replace migration.
What is a control plane?

In a hybrid platform like Cloudera Anywhere Cloud, the control plane is the centralized management and orchestration layer that handles administration, governance, and provisioning, while remaining architecturally separated from where the actual data is stored and processed. Think of it as the "command center" or single pane of glass for your entire data and AI ecosystem.
Brian Rosso, CRO, Cloudera

Chief Revenue Officer Rosso and SVP for the APJ region Remus Lim stated that this hybrid pull is even sharper in Asia-Pacific than in the US or Europe, where sovereignty concerns and regulatory divergence between markets are colliding with a region that, in Lim's telling, had moved to public cloud more cautiously in the first place and is now actively building hybrid architecture as a first choice rather than a retreat.

Sansbury framed the underlying economics bluntly - enterprises that took large amounts of free hyperscaler credit in the early cloud years are increasingly viewing that credit the way he described it – ‘like a free kitten’, i.e., attractive on the surface, but carrying real long-term cost once workloads are locked in.
Modular Pricing, The Mid-market, And The Partner Build-out

Rosso and Lim spent much of the discussion on mentioning Cloudera's push into the mid-market, which the company has historically avoided because its platform was too heavy and expensive for smaller deployments.

The new modular architecture is designed to change that, per Rosso. Customers can now license individual data services rather than buying the full platform, which the company believes opens a real mid-market opportunity it previously ceded. This opens up a new market for Cloudera.

On partnerships, AWS was cited as a dominant channel. Rosso referenced a figure of roughly 77 per cent of business flowing through partner-led motions, with AWS singled out specifically. Separately, the APAC SVP described a newly formed ‘Applied AI’ team, i.e., one team of data scientists and one team of deploy engineers per region, including Japan, dedicated purely to AI use cases and to driving AI adoption through fast proof-of-concept work, distinct from Cloudera's pre-sales engineering organisation.
In focus: Reemus Lim, SVP, APJ, Cloudera

On the FY27 outlook, Rosso declined to give specific revenue guidance but described the previous financial year ‘phenomenal’ and pointed to a large, unnamed public energy company - described as one of the largest in the world, operating across roughly 150 countries - as Anywhere Cloud's flagship design partner heading into general availability. He described India as a top market from a growth perspective and mentioned multiple RFPs (Request for Proposal) from companies “with numbers of customers more than some countries' population”.
The Era Of Edge Computing

Both Gago and Lim flagged edge inferencing as a fast-growing area, distinct from the core hybrid cloud story, i.e., use cases where decisions must be made at the point data is created because connectivity cannot be guaranteed, such as offshore oil and gas operations, industrial IoT predictive maintenance, and what Abhas Ricky later called physical AI, i.e., robotics and sensor-driven decision-making.

Lim cited work with an unnamed cybersecurity technology partner using Cloudera's edge capabilities to process device telemetry in real time, and separate work building bespoke IoT platforms with an industrial partner for predictive maintenance.
The India Angle

When asked directly what share of Cloudera's overall revenue India represents, Sansbury's answered that India represents ‘a lot of growth opportunity’ for Cloudera. Prior to Evolve26, Sansbury had visited India and emphasised its importance as both a growth market and a critical R&D hub. Currently, India's share of global revenue is still in single digits as a percentage of the total.
He ranked Cloudera's largest markets globally, in order, as North America first, Western Europe second, and Asia-Pacific starting to close the gap behind them.
Within that ranking, he suggested India stands as the third or fourth largest market in APAC.

This lines up directionally with what Rosso said independently, without prompting from the India question in the CEO session. He called India "probably one of the top three markets from a growth perspective.” He cited one unnamed Indian customer whose end-user base is larger than the population of several countries combined, by way of illustrating the scale of data volumes Cloudera is handling in the market.

Additionally, several Indian institutions were named among the customer delegation at EVOLVE26 Singapore, including Axis Bank, Bombay Stock Exchange, IDFC First Bank, Yes Bank, ICICI Securities, Reliance Industries, PhonePe, and Bharti Airtel, consistent with the banking-and-fintech-heavy India customer base Rosso described.
Where Does AI Go Next?

CBO Abhas Ricky’s central argument is interesting. He stated that transformer-based models are architecturally limited, i.e., they generate outputs based on patterns in their training data and cannot genuinely reason about situations outside that distribution.

He predicted the next wave of foundation models will move beyond general-purpose transformers toward domain-specific scientific models built on different underlying architectures: physics-based foundation models, biology-based foundation models (citing unnamed peer companies already building these for drug discovery), and chemistry-based foundation models for materials science and experimental design, the latter built around atomic and molecular composition rather than token prediction.

He argued this trend, if it plays out, actually strengthens Cloudera's position rather than threatening it, because these domain-specific models will still depend on proprietary, contextual private data to be useful. He emphasised a statistic - that 74 per cent of all data still sits within private environments, i.e., outside the public cloud - as the reason inference will increasingly need to run where that data already resides, which he described as Cloudera's core value proposition.

He illustrated the point with an example of an unnamed industrial customer doing smoke detection via sensor data, which he expects to migrate toward physics-based simulation models that still need to run inference at the edge, near the sensors themselves.

Beyond domain-specific models, Ricky named memory or context window as the next major frontier for AI generally, i.e., the ability of a system to retain context and experience across sessions, tools and platforms the way humans do, rather than starting fresh in every new conversation.
What ‘memory’ is being talked about here?

This is not random access memory or RAM that is being talked about here. This is a reference to content window. A context window is the maximum amount of text an artificial intelligence model can process and remember during a single interaction.

He described this as one of the most significant remaining gaps between current AI systems and human cognition, distinguishing between memory of a single prompt or session and something closer to persistent, transferable context across an organisation's tools and systems.
The Moat? According To Cloudera, Not The Product, The Data

The CEO was asked directly whether Anywhere Cloud is Cloudera’s current point of differentiation, and whether any competitor offers something comparable. Ricky jumped in and elaborated that he does not believe any rival can currently match a single platform spanning workload management, governance and portability across multiple infrastructure environments in a comparable timeframe.
Abhas Ricky, CBO and GM, Applied AI, Cloudera
He was, however, careful to add that Cloudera has to keep innovating on the product itself to stay ahead.

Ricky located Cloudera's deeper, more durable advantage for us, i.e., not the Anywhere Cloud product, but roughly 30 exabytes of accumulated, mission-critical enterprise data sitting in customer lakehouses.
What is a Lakehouse?

A data lake is a centralized cloud storage repository that holds large amounts of raw data in its original format until you need it. Unlike traditional databases that require data to be cleaned and structured first, a data lake accepts everything right away.
A data lakehouse is a modern cloud data storage design that combines the low-cost, flexible storage of a data lake with the fast query performance and management features of a data warehouse.

His example was that a bank's treasury transaction data is categorically different from, and far harder to replicate quickly than, generic reporting data. He argued that depth and specificity of historical, operational data is effectively impossible for a new entrant to reproduce, and framed it as Cloudera's most durable competitive advantage, ahead of any individual product.

On monetisation, he framed the industry's shared long-term direction as compute and inference consumption becoming the standard unit by which AI products are measured and monetised, with GPU and chip capacity itself becoming the next major constraint for large technology players.

Ricky and Sansbury described the control plane as built on established open-source foundations, i.e., Apache Ranger for fine-grained access policy enforcement, and what is very likely Apache Atlas for lineage and metadata, with the Octopai-derived lineage and auditability layer, previously available only as a public-cloud SaaS product, now being extended to private and air-gapped environments to complete the hybrid governance picture.
